summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding is documented for Córdoba. A trans visitor here stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America, and is assessed against the national position on lethal violence rather than against any local deviation.

Nothing about being trans is criminalised. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

The formal framework does not describe what trans people encounter in practice. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, 32, a trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, showing her flailing in a creek unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands. She died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." Thirteen trans people were killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. The national pattern is that lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, be filmed, and leave the perpetrator unarrested.

Some of that targeting is organised. In Caquetá department armed groups ran a "social cleansing" campaign, with flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend was killed. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024, discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and killings of queer Colombians have continued after the Millerey case as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict. The pattern is territorial violence and displacement of trans people by armed actors.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry, partner recognition and access to premises are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country; same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises.
tangentialFactors:
The distance between the statutory position and lived experience is the central turbulence factor for a visitor. Colombia's recognition, marriage and facilities jurisprudence are among the strongest in Latin America, yet 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025 alone and the Attorney General's Office logged 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025; the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission framed this as institutional progress disconnected from daily life.

The two incident records that carry the pattern sit in other departments: Antioquia for the filmed daylight killing of Sara Millerey in April 2025, with no arrest recorded after a presidential order, and Caquetá for armed-group flyer campaigns driving a trans election candidate out of town in 2024. Neither is a Córdoba finding, but both indicate what armed-actor violence against trans women looks like in the region and what an investigation can be expected to yield.

Occupational squeeze narrows the visible surface for trans women nationally: discrimination is reported to limit them mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which concentrates exposure to the same armed groups running "social cleansing" campaigns and to street-level policing.

Guajira's kill-list flyers, circulating since March 2024 with named individuals, show that threat lists against trans people are a live method of coercion in the country rather than a closed episode.
localsOnly:
Residents face a dense set of domestic entitlements. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Correctional treatment is governed by court order: a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

Family law is settled for residents as well. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and same-sex marriages performed abroad must be registered by notaries and registrars under a National Registry memo.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than judicial: a notarial document suffices, with no surgical, psychiatric or judicial prerequisite, and the resulting identity documents can carry "trans" or "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

No Córdoba-specific source is present in the inventory. Whether the department has recorded trans-related hate-crime prosecutions, police complaints, or threats from armed groups is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" identity-document markers are being issued at registry offices in Córdoba is unresolved; the sources date the national rule but do not record departmental implementation.

The inventory gives national killing totals without a departmental breakdown. How many of the 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, or the 35 LGBTI murders recorded between January and May 2025, occurred in Córdoba is not sourced.

Reports of a second trans woman's friend being killed in Caquetá, and of a trans rough-sleeper's stabbing death, are undated and unattributed to a department in the source material; they are carried as part of the national pattern only.

Whether the 2016 Ministry of Interior decree's procedural obligations have been implemented by departmental bodies in Córdoba is not addressed by any source in the inventory.
